Knowledge Sharing知识共享

Chapter 3. Knowledge Sharing · 第 3 章 · 知识共享

Written by Nina Chen and Mark Barolak; Edited by Riona MacNamara.

作者：Nina Chen、Mark Barolak；编辑：Riona MacNamara。

Your organization understands your problem domain better than some random person on the internet; your organization should be able to answer most of its own questions. To achieve that, you need both experts who know the answers to those questions and mechanisms to distribute their knowledge, which is what we’ll explore in this chapter. These mechanisms range from the utterly simple (Ask questions; Write down what you know) to the much more structured, such as tutorials and classes. Most importantly, however, your organization needs a culture of learning, and that requires creating the psychological safety that permits people to admit to a lack of knowledge.

你的组织比互联网上某个随机路人更懂自己的问题域；你的组织应当能够回答自己的大多数问题。要做到这一点，你既需要知道这些问题答案的专家，也需要分发他们知识的机制——这正是本章要探讨的内容。这些机制从极其简单（提问；把你知道的写下来），到结构化得多的形式（如教程与课程）不等。然而最重要的是，你的组织需要一种学习的文化，而这就需要创造心理安全感，允许人们承认自己知识不足。

Challenges to Learning · 学习面临的挑战

Sharing expertise across an organization is not an easy task. Without a strong culture of learning, challenges can emerge. Google has experienced a number of these challenges, especially as the company has scaled:

在整个组织内部分享专长并非易事。没有强大的学习文化，各种挑战就会冒出来。Google 经历过其中不少挑战，尤其是在公司扩张的过程中：

  • Lack of psychological safety: An environment in which people are afraid to take risks or make mistakes in front of others because they fear being punished for it. This often manifests as a culture of fear or a tendency to avoid transparency.

    缺乏心理安全：一种让人们害怕冒险、害怕在别人面前犯错的环境，因为他们担心因此受到惩罚。它常表现为恐惧文化，或回避透明的倾向。

  • Information islands: Knowledge fragmentation that occurs in different parts of an organization that don’t communicate with one another or use shared resources. In such an environment, each group develops its own way of doing things.

    信息孤岛：当组织中不同部分互不沟通、也不共享资源时所发生的知识碎片化。在这种环境里，每个群体都发展出自己一套做事方式。

原书第 71 页

  • Information fragmentation: Each island has an incomplete picture of the bigger whole.

    信息碎片化：每个孤岛对更大的整体都只有一幅不完整的图景。

  • Information duplication: Each island has reinvented its own way of doing something.

    信息重复：每个孤岛都重新发明了自己做某件事的方式。

  • Information skew: Each island has its own ways of doing the same thing, and these might or might not conflict.

    信息偏差：每个孤岛都有自己做同一件事的方式，而这些方式可能一致、也可能冲突。

  • Single point of failure (SPOF): A bottleneck that occurs when critical information is available from only a single person. SPOFs can arise out of good intentions: it can be easy to fall into a habit of “Let me take care of that for you.” But this approach optimizes for short-term efficiency (“It’s faster for me to do it”) at the cost of poor long-term scalability (the team never learns how to do whatever it is that needs to be done).

    单点故障（SPOF）：当关键信息只能从一个人那里获得时所形成的瓶颈。SPOF 也可能出于好意而产生：人们很容易养成“这事让我来帮你处理吧”的习惯。但这种做法是为短期效率（“我来做更快”）优化，代价却是长期扩展性差（团队永远学不会该怎么去做那件事）。

  • All-or-nothing expertise: A group of people that is split between people who know “everything” and novices, with little middle ground. This problem often reinforces itself if experts always do everything themselves and don’t take the time to develop new experts through mentoring or documentation.

    全有或全无的专长：一群人被分裂成“什么都懂”的人与新手两类，中间地带很薄。如果专家总是自己包办一切、不愿花时间通过带教或文档培养新专家，这个问题往往会自我强化。

  • Parroting: Mimicry without understanding. This is typically characterized by mindlessly copying patterns or code without understanding their purpose, often under the assumption that said code is needed for unknown reasons.

    鹦鹉学舌：不理解的模仿。其典型特征是：不动脑子地照搬模式或代码，却不理解其用途，往往假定这段代码出于某些未知的原因是必需的。

  • Haunted graveyards: Places, often in code, that people avoid touching or changing because they are afraid that something might go wrong. Unlike the aforementioned parroting, haunted graveyards are characterized by people avoiding action because of fear and superstition.

    闹鬼的墓地：人们因为害怕出问题而不敢触碰或修改的地方（常在代码里）。与上述鹦鹉学舌不同，“闹鬼的墓地”的特征是：人们因恐惧与迷信而回避行动。

原书第 72 页

In the rest of this chapter, we dive into strategies that Google’s engineering organizations have found to be successful in addressing these challenges.

在本章余下部分，我们将深入探讨 Google 各工程组织在应对这些挑战上被证明行之有效的策略。

Philosophy · 理念

Software engineering can be defined as the multiperson development of multiversion programs. People are at the core of software engineering: code is an important output but only a small part of building a product. Crucially, code does not emerge spontaneously out of nothing, and neither does expertise. Every expert was once a novice: an organization’s success depends on growing and investing in its people.

软件工程可以被定义为“多人对多版本程序的开发”。人是软件工程的核心：代码是重要的产出，但只是构建产品的一小部分。关键在于，代码不会凭空自发产生，专长也不会。每个专家都曾是新手：一个组织的成功，取决于它如何培养并投资于人。

Personalized, one-to-one advice from an expert is always invaluable. Different team members have different areas of expertise, and so the best teammate to ask for any given question will vary. But if the expert goes on vacation or switches teams, the team can be left in the lurch. And although one person might be able to provide personalized help for one-to-many, this doesn’t scale and is limited to small numbers of “many.”

专家给出的个性化、一对一建议总是无价的。不同团队成员有不同的专长领域，因此对任何一个具体问题，最该去问的队友都不一样。但如果那位专家去度假或换了团队，团队就可能陷入无人可问的窘境。而且，尽管一个人也许能为“一对多”提供个性化帮助，但这不可扩展，且仅限于数量很小的“多”。

Documented knowledge, on the other hand, can better scale not just to the team but to the entire organization. Mechanisms such as a team wiki enable many authors to share their expertise with a larger group. But even though written documentation is more scalable than one-to-one conversations, that scalability comes with some trade-offs: it might be more generalized and less applicable to individual learners’ situations, and it comes with the added maintenance cost required to keep information relevant and up to date over time.

另一方面，写下来的知识不仅能更好地扩展到团队、还能扩展到整个组织。像团队 wiki 这样的机制，让众多作者能与更大的群体分享专长。不过，尽管书面文档比一对一对话更可扩展，这种可扩展性也伴随着一些权衡：它可能更泛化、对个体学习者的具体情境适用性更差，而且还要付出额外的维护成本，以让信息随时间保持相关与更新。

Tribal knowledge exists in the gap between what individual team members know and what is documented. Human experts know these things that aren’t written down. If we document that knowledge and maintain it, it is now available not only to somebody with direct one-to-one access to the expert today, but to anybody who can find and view the documentation.

部落知识（tribal knowledge）存在于“团队成员个人所知”与“被记录下来的内容”之间的缝隙里。人类专家知道这些没被写下来的东西。如果我们把这些知识记录下来并维护它，那么如今它不仅对某个能一对一直接找到专家的人可用，也对任何能找到并查看文档的人可用。

So in a magical world in which everything is always perfectly and immediately documented, we wouldn’t need to consult a person any more, right? Not quite. Written knowledge has scaling advantages, but so does targeted human help. A human expert can synthesize their expanse of knowledge. They can assess what information is applicable to the individual’s use case, determine whether the documentation is still relevant, and know where to find it. Or, if they don’t know where to find the answers, they might know who does.

那么，在一个一切都被完美、即时记录下来的神奇世界里，我们就不再需要请教人了，对吧？并非如此。书面知识有可扩展的优势，但有针对性的人类帮助也有其优势。一位人类专家能综合他广博的知识。他能判断哪些信息适用于这个人的用例、判断文档是否仍然相关、并知道去哪里找答案。或者，如果他不知道答案在哪，他也许知道谁知道。

原书第 73 页

Tribal and written knowledge complement each other. Even a perfectly expert team with perfect documentation needs to communicate with one another, coordinate with other teams, and adapt their strategies over time. No single knowledge-sharing approach is the correct solution for all types of learning, and the particulars of a good mix will likely vary based on your organization. Institutional knowledge evolves over time, and the knowledge-sharing methods that work best for your organization will likely change as it grows. Train, focus on learning and growth, and build your own stable of experts: there is no such thing as too much engineering expertise.

部落知识与书面知识互为补充。即便是一支拥有完美文档的完美专家团队，也仍然需要彼此沟通、与其他团队协调、随时间调整策略。没有哪一种单一的知识共享方法是适用于一切学习类型的正确解，而一个好的组合的具体配比，很可能因组织而异。制度知识随时间演进，对你组织最有效的知识共享方式，也很可能随它成长而改变。去培训、聚焦学习与成长、建立你自己的专家队伍：工程专长再多也不嫌多。

Setting the Stage: Psychological Safety · 铺垫舞台：心理安全

Psychological safety is critical to promoting a learning environment. To learn, you must first acknowledge that there are things you don’t understand. We should welcome such honesty rather than punish it. (Google does this pretty well, but sometimes engineers are reluctant to admit they don’t understand something.) An enormous part of learning is being able to try things and feeling safe to fail. In a healthy environment, people feel comfortable asking questions, being wrong, and learning new things. This is a baseline expectation for all Google teams; indeed, our research has shown that psychological safety is the most important part of an effective team.

心理安全对于培育学习环境至关重要。要学习，你必须先承认存在你不懂的东西。我们应当欢迎这种诚实，而不是惩罚它。（Google 在这点上做得相当不错，但有时工程师仍不愿承认自己不懂某件事。）学习的一大部分，就是能够去尝试、并感到失败是安全的。在一个健康的环境里，人们能自在地提问、犯错、学习新东西。这是对所有 Google 团队的基线期望；事实上，我们的研究表明，心理安全是高效团队最重要的组成部分。

Mentorship · 导师制

At Google, we try to set the tone as soon as a “Noogler” (new Googler) engineer joins the company. One important way of building psychological safety is to assign Nooglers a mentor—someone who is not their team member, manager, or tech lead—whose responsibilities explicitly include answering questions and helping the Noogler ramp up. Having an officially assigned mentor to ask for help makes it easier for the newcomer and means that they don’t need to worry about taking up too much of their coworkers’ time.

在 Google，我们努力在“Noogler”（新 Googler）工程师刚加入公司时就定下基调。建立心理安全的一个重要方式，是给 Noogler 配一位导师——一位既非其团队成员、也非其经理或技术负责人的人——其职责明确包括答疑、帮助 Noogler 上手。有一位正式指派的导师可以求助，让新人更容易开口，也意味着他们不必担心占用同事太多时间。

A mentor is a volunteer who has been at Google for more than a year and who is available to advise on anything from using Google infrastructure to navigating Google culture. Crucially, the mentor is there to be a safety net to talk to if the mentee doesn’t know whom else to ask for advice. This mentor is not on the same team as the mentee, which can make the mentee feel more comfortable about asking for help in tricky situations.

导师是在 Google 工作一年以上的志愿者，可就从使用 Google 基础设施到适应 Google 文化的任何事情提供建议。关键在于，当被指导者不知道还能向谁请教时，导师就是那张可以倾诉的安全网。导师与被指导者不在同一团队，这能让后者在棘手情境下更自在地求助。

Mentorship formalizes and facilitates learning, but learning itself is an ongoing process. There will always be opportunities for coworkers to learn from one another, whether it’s a new employee joining the organization or an experienced engineer learning a new technology. With a healthy team, teammates will be open not just to

导师制把学习正式化、便利化，但学习本身是一个持续的过程。同事之间总有互相学习的机会——无论是新员工加入组织，还是资深工程师学习一项新技术。在一个健康的团队里，队友们不仅乐于

原书第 74 页

answering but also to asking questions: showing that they don’t know something and learning from one another.

回答问题，也乐于提问：展现自己不知道某事，并彼此学习。

Psychological Safety in Large Groups · 大群体中的心理安全

Asking a nearby teammate for help is easier than approaching a large group of mostly strangers. But as we’ve seen, one-to-one solutions don’t scale well. Group solutions are more scalable, but they are also scarier. It can be intimidating for novices to form a question and ask it of a large group, knowing that their question might be archived for many years. The need for psychological safety is amplified in large groups. Every member of the group has a role to play in creating and maintaining a safe environment that ensures that newcomers are confident asking questions and up-and-coming experts feel empowered to help those newcomers without the fear of having their answers attacked by established experts.

向附近的队友求助，比向一大群基本是陌生人的人开口容易。但正如我们所见，一对一的方案扩展性不佳。群体方案更可扩展，却也更吓人。对新手来说，组织一个问题、向一个大群体提出，是令人胆怯的——尤其知道自己的问题可能被存档许多年。在大群体中，对心理安全的需求被放大了。群体的每一个成员，在创造并维护一个安全环境方面都有一份角色要扮演：这个环境要确保新人有信心提问，也要让成长中的专家感到自己有权帮助这些新人，而不必担心自己的回答被资深专家攻击。

The most important way to achieve this safe and welcoming environment is for group interactions to be cooperative, not adversarial. Table 3-1 lists some examples of recommended patterns (and their corresponding antipatterns) of group interactions.

要实现这种安全而热情的环境，最重要的方式是让群体互动是合作式的、而非对抗式的。表 3-1 列出了群体互动中推荐模式（及其对应的反模式）的一些例子。

Recommended patterns (cooperative) 推荐模式（合作式）Antipatterns (adversarial) 反模式（对抗式）
Basic questions or mistakes are guided in the proper direction.

基础问题或错误会被引导向正确方向。

Basic questions or mistakes are picked on, and the person asking the question is chastised.

基础问题或错误被揪着不放，提问者遭到斥责。

Explanations are given with the intent of helping the person asking the question learn.

给出解释时意在帮助提问者学习。

Explanations are given with the intent of showing off one’s own knowledge.

给出解释时意在炫耀自己的知识。

Responses are kind, patient, and helpful.

回应友善、耐心、有帮助。

Responses are condescending, snarky, and unconstructive.

回应居高临下、带讽刺、毫无建设性。

Interactions are shared discussions for finding solutions.

互动是为寻找解决方案而展开的共同讨论。

Interactions are arguments with “winners” and “losers.”

互动是有“赢家”和“输家”的争吵。

Table 3-1. Group interaction patterns

表 3-1 · 群体互动模式

These antipatterns can emerge unintentionally: someone might be trying to be helpful but is accidentally condescending and unwelcoming. We find the Recurse Center’s social rules to be helpful here:

这些反模式可能在不经意间出现：有人也许是想帮忙，却不小心显得居高临下、不受欢迎。我们发现 Recurse Center 的社交规则在这里很有帮助：

  • No feigned surprise (“What?! I can’t believe you don’t know what the stack is!”). Feigned surprise is a barrier to psychological safety and makes members of the group afraid of admitting to a lack of knowledge.

    不要假装惊讶（“什么？！真不敢相信你居然不知道栈是什么！”）。假装惊讶是心理安全的障碍，会让群体成员害怕承认自己知识不足。

  • No “well-actuallys.” Pedantic corrections that tend to be about grandstanding rather than precision.

    不要“其实是这样的（well-actually）”。那种卖弄学问的纠正，往往是为了显摆、而非为了精确。

  • No back-seat driving. Interrupting an existing discussion to offer opinions without committing to the conversation.

    不要“后座司机”。在不真正投入对话的情况下，打断既有讨论、只抛观点。

原书第 75 页

  • No subtle “-isms” (“It’s so easy my grandmother could do it!”). Small expressions of bias (racism, ageism, homophobia) that can make individuals feel unwelcome, disrespected, or unsafe.

    不要微妙的“偏见腔”（“这简单到我奶奶都能做！”）。那些细小的偏见流露（种族主义、年龄歧视、恐同），会让人感到不受欢迎、不被尊重或不安全。

Growing Your Knowledge · 增长你自己的知识

Knowledge sharing starts with yourself. It is important to recognize that you always have something to learn. The following guidelines allow you to augment your own personal knowledge.

知识共享从你自己开始。重要的是要认识到：你总有可学之物。下面这些指引能帮你扩充自己的个人知识。

Ask Questions · 多提问

If you take away only a single thing from this chapter, it is this: always be learning; always be asking questions.

如果你从这一章只带走一件事，那就是：永远在学习，永远在提问。

We tell Nooglers that ramping up can take around six months. This extended period is necessary to ramp up on Google’s large, complex infrastructure, but it also reinforces the idea that learning is an ongoing, iterative process. One of the biggest mistakes that beginners make is not to ask for help when they’re stuck. You might be tempted to struggle through it alone or feel fearful that your questions are “too simple.” “I just need to try harder before I ask anyone for help,” you think. Don’t fall into this trap! Your coworkers are often the best source of information: leverage this valuable resource.

我们告诉 Noogler，上手大约需要六个月。这段较长的时间对于熟悉 Google 庞大复杂的基础设施是必要的，但它也强化了这样一个观念：学习是一个持续迭代的过程。新手犯的最大错误之一，就是卡住时不去求助。你也许会想独自硬扛，或害怕自己的问题“太简单”。你心里想：“我再努力试试，实在不行再找人帮忙。”别掉进这个陷阱！你的同事往往是最好的信息来源：好好利用这个宝贵资源。

There is no magical day when you suddenly always know exactly what to do in every situation—there’s always more to learn. Engineers who have been at Google for years still have areas in which they don’t feel like they know what they are doing, and that’s OK! Don’t be afraid to say “I don’t know what that is; could you explain it?” Embrace not knowing things as an area of opportunity rather than one to fear. It doesn’t matter whether you’re new to a team or a senior leader: you should always be in an environment in which there’s something to learn. If not, you stagnate (and should find a new environment).

不存在某个神奇的日子，让你突然在一切情境下都确切知道该做什么——总有更多可学。在 Google 干了多年的工程师，仍有一些领域觉得自己摸不着头脑，而这没关系！别害怕说：“我不知道那是什么，你能解释一下吗？”把“不知道”当作机会所在，而不是恐惧所在。无论你是团队新人还是资深领导者都一样：你应当始终身处一个有东西可学的环境。如果不是，你就在停滞（那就该换个环境）。

It’s especially critical for those in leadership roles to model this behavior: it’s important not to mistakenly equate “seniority” with “knowing everything.” In fact, the more you know, the more you know you don’t know. Openly asking questions or expressing gaps in knowledge reinforces that it’s OK for others to do the same.

对担任领导职务的人来说，以身作则地展现这种行为尤其关键：重要的是别错误地把“资历深”等同于“什么都知道”。事实上，你知道得越多，就越知道自己不知道什么。公开提问或坦承知识空白，会强化这样一个信号：别人也可以这样做。

原书第 76 页

On the receiving end, patience and kindness when answering questions fosters an environment in which people feel safe looking for help. Making it easier to overcome the initial hesitation to ask a question sets the tone early: reach out to solicit questions, and make it easy for even “trivial” questions to get an answer. Although engineers could probably figure out tribal knowledge on their own, they’re not here to work in a vacuum. Targeted help allows engineers to be productive faster, which in turn makes their entire team more productive.

在回答问题的另一端，耐心与友善能培育出一种让人敢于求助的环境。让人更容易克服提问最初的犹豫，能早早定下基调：主动伸手去征集问题，让哪怕是“鸡毛蒜皮”的问题也容易得到回答。尽管工程师大概自己也能搞懂那些部落知识，但他们不是来真空里工作的。有针对性的帮助让工程师更快进入产出状态，进而让整个团队更有生产力。

Understand Context · 理解上下文

Learning is not just about understanding new things; it also includes developing an understanding of the decisions behind the design and implementation of existing things. Suppose that your team inherits a legacy codebase for a critical piece of infrastructure that has existed for many years. The original authors are long gone, and the code is difficult to understand. It can be tempting to rewrite from scratch rather than spend time learning the existing code. But instead of thinking “I don’t get it” and ending your thoughts there, dive deeper: what questions should you be asking? Consider the principle of “Chesterton’s fence”: before removing or changing something, first understand why it’s there.

学习不仅是理解新事物，还包括去理解现有事物在设计与实现背后的那些决策。假设你的团队继承了一个关键基础设施的遗留代码库，它已经存在多年。原作者早已离开，代码又难以理解。这时人们很容易想推倒重写，而不愿花时间学习现有代码。但与其想“我搞不懂”就到此为止，不如深入下去：你应该问哪些问题？想想“切斯特顿的栅栏（Chesterton’s fence）”原则：在移除或改动某样东西之前，先理解它为什么在那里。

In the matter of reforming things, as distinct from deforming them, there
is one plain and simple principle; a principle which will probably be called a
paradox. There exists in such a case a certain institution or law; let us say,
for the sake of simplicity, a fence or gate erected across a road. The more
modern type of reformer goes gaily up to it and says, "I don’t see the use of
this; let us clear it away." To which the more intelligent type of reformer
will do well to answer: "If you don’t see the use of it, I certainly won’t let
you clear it away. Go away and think. Then, when you can come back and tell me
that you do see the use of it, I may allow you to destroy it."

This doesn’t mean that code can’t lack clarity or that existing design patterns can’t be wrong, but engineers have a tendency to reach for “this is bad!” far more quickly than is often warranted, especially for unfamiliar code, languages, or paradigms. Google is not immune to this. Seek out and understand context, especially for decisions that seem unusual. After you’ve understood the context and purpose of the code, consider whether your change still makes sense. If it does, go ahead and make it; if it doesn’t, document your reasoning for future readers. Many Google style guides explicitly include context to help readers understand the rationale behind the style guidelines instead of just memorizing a list of arbitrary rules. More subtly, understanding the rationale behind a given guideline allows authors to make informed decisions about when the guideline shouldn’t apply or whether the guideline needs updating. (See Chapter 8.)

这并不意味着代码不可能不够清晰、或现有设计模式不可能有错；但工程师有一种倾向：动不动就喊“这太糟了！”，而且往往喊得太快，尤其是面对不熟悉的代码、语言或范式时。Google 也不能免俗。去寻找并理解上下文，尤其是那些看起来不寻常的决策。在你理解了代码的上下文与意图之后，再想想你的改动是否仍然合理。如果合理，就尽管去做；如果不合理，就把你的理由写下来，留给后来的读者。Google 的许多风格指南都明确包含上下文，帮助读者理解风格指南背后的 rationale，而不是死记一套任意规则。更微妙的是，理解某条指南背后的道理，能让作者在“这条指南何时不该适用”或“是否需要更新”上做出知情判断。（见第 8 章。）

Scaling Your Questions: Ask the Community · 扩展你的提问：向社区求助

Getting one-to-one help is high bandwidth but necessarily limited in scale. And as a learner, it can be difficult to remember every detail. Do your future self a favor: when you learn something from a one-to-one discussion, write it down. Chances are that future newcomers will have the same questions you had. Do them a favor, too, and share what you write down.

获得一对一帮助带宽很高，但规模必然受限。而作为学习者，要记住每一个细节也很难。帮未来的自己一个忙：当你从一次一对一讨论中学到东西时，把它写下来。很可能未来的新人会有和你一样的问题。也帮他们一个忙，把你写下的东西分享出去。

Although sharing the answers you receive can be useful, it’s also beneficial to seek help not from individuals but from the greater community. In this section, we examine different forms of community-based learning. Each of these approaches—group chats, mailing lists, and question-and-answer systems—have different trade-offs and complement one another. But each of them enables the knowledge seeker to get help from a broader community of peers and experts and also ensures that answers are broadly available to current and future members of that community.

分享你得到的答案固然有用，但不从个人、而从更大的社区寻求帮助也同样有益。在本节，我们考察不同形式的社区式学习。这些方式——群聊、邮件列表、问答系统——各有不同权衡、互为补充。但它们每一种都让求知者能从更广大的同行与专家社区获得帮助，也确保答案能被该社区现在和未来的成员广泛获取。

Group Chats · 群聊

When you have a question, it can sometimes be difficult to get help from the right person. Maybe you’re not sure who knows the answer, or the person you want to ask is busy. In these situations, group chats are great, because you can ask your question to many people at once and have a quick back-and-forth conversation with whoever is available. As a bonus, other members of the group chat can learn from the question and answer, and many forms of group chat can be automatically archived and searched later. Group chats tend to be devoted either to topics or to teams. Topic-driven group chats are typically open so that anyone can drop in to ask a question. They tend to attract experts and can grow quite large, so questions are usually answered quickly. Team-oriented chats, on the other hand, tend to be smaller and restrict membership. As a result, they might not have the same reach as a topic-driven chat, but their smaller size can feel safer to a newcomer.

当你有一个问题时，有时很难从对的人那里得到帮助。也许你不确定谁知道答案，也许你想问的人正忙。在这些情况下，群聊很棒，因为你可以同时向很多人提问，并和任何有空的人快速一来一回地对话。额外收获是，群聊的其他成员也能从这个问答中学到东西，而且许多形式的群聊会被自动存档、日后可搜索。群聊要么按主题、要么按团队组织。按主题的群聊通常是开放的，任何人都能进来提问。它们往往吸引专家、可能变得很大，所以问题通常很快得到回答。而按团队的聊天往往较小、限制成员。结果是，它们的覆盖面可能不如按主题的聊天，但较小的规模让新人感到更安全。

Although group chats are great for quick questions, they don’t provide much structure, which can make it difficult to extract meaningful information from a conversation in which you’re not actively involved. As soon as you need to share information outside of the group, or make it available to refer back to later, you should write a document or email a mailing list.

尽管群聊很适合快速问题，但它提供不了多少结构，这使得从一场你并未积极参与的对话中提取有意义的信息变得困难。一旦你需要把信息分享到群外、或让它日后可以回查，你就应该写一份文档，或给邮件列表发邮件。

Mailing Lists · 邮件列表

Most topics at Google have a topic-users@ or topic-discuss@ Google Groups mailing list that anyone at the company can join or email. Asking a question on a public mailing list is a lot like asking a group chat: the question reaches a lot of people who could

Google 的大多数主题都有一个 topic-users@ 或 topic-discuss@ 的 Google Groups 邮件列表，公司里任何人都能加入或发信。在公开邮件列表上提问，很像在群聊里提问：问题会到达很多可能

potentially answer it and anyone following the list can learn from the answer. Unlike group chats, though, public mailing lists are easy to share with a wider audience: they are packaged into searchable archives, and email threads provide more structure than group chats. At Google, mailing lists are also indexed and can be discovered by Moma, Google’s intranet search engine. When you find an answer to a question you asked on a mailing list, it can be tempting to get on with your work. Don’t do it! You never know when someone will need the same information in the future, so it’s a best practice to post the answer back to the list.

回答它的人，而任何订阅该列表的人都能从答案中学到东西。不过与群聊不同，公开邮件列表很容易分享给更广泛的受众：它们被打包进可搜索的存档，而且邮件线程比群聊提供更多结构。在 Google，邮件列表还会被索引、可以通过 Google 内网搜索引擎 Moma 检索到。当你找到自己在邮件列表上所问问题的答案时，很想赶紧继续干活。别这样！你永远不知道将来什么时候会有人需要同样的信息，所以把答案回贴到列表上是最佳实践。

Mailing lists are not without their trade-offs. They’re well suited for complicated questions that require a lot of context, but they’re clumsy for the quick back-and-forth exchanges at which group chats excel. A thread about a particular problem is generally most useful while it is active. Email archives are immutable, and it can be hard to determine whether an answer discovered in an old discussion thread is still relevant to a present-day situation. Additionally, the signal-to-noise ratio can be lower than other mediums like formal documentation because the problem that someone is having with their specific workflow might not be applicable to you.

邮件列表也并非没有权衡。它很适合需要大量上下文的复杂问题，但在群聊擅长的那种快速来回交流上显得笨拙。一个关于特定问题的线程，通常在它活跃时最有用。邮件存档是不可变的，而在一条旧讨论线程里找到的答案，是否仍适用于今天的情境，往往很难判断。此外，它的信噪比可能低于正式文档等其他媒介，因为某人在其特定工作流中遇到的问题，未必适用于你。

Email at Google: Google culture is infamously email-centric and email-heavy. Google engineers receive hundreds of emails (if not more) each day, with varying degrees of actionability. Google tends toward email-based workflows by default. This isn’t necessarily because email is a better medium than other communications options—it often isn’t—rather, it’s because that’s what our culture is accustomed to. Keep this in mind as your organization considers what forms of communication to encourage or invest in.

Google 的邮件：Google 文化以邮件为中心、邮件量大而“臭名昭著”。Google 工程师每天收到数百封（甚至更多）邮件，可行动程度不一。Google 默认倾向于基于邮件的工作流。这未必是因为邮件比其他沟通媒介更好——它往往并不好——而更多是因为这是我们文化所习惯的。当你的组织考虑该鼓励或投资哪些沟通形式时，请记住这一点。

YAQS (“Yet Another Question System”) is a Google-internal version of a Stack Overflow–like website, making it easy for Googlers to link to existing or work-in-progress code as well as discuss confidential information. Like Stack Overflow, YAQS shares many of the same advantages of mailing lists and adds refinements: answers marked as helpful are promoted in the user interface, and

YAQS（“又一个问答系统”）是 Google 内部版的 Stack Overflow 式网站，让 Googler 能方便地链接到已有或正在开发中的代码，并讨论机密信息。和 Stack Overflow 一样，YAQS 兼具邮件列表的许多优点，并做了改进：被标记为有用的回答会在界面上被提升展示，而且

users can edit questions and answers so that they remain accurate and useful as code and facts change. As a result, some mailing lists have been superseded by YAQS, whereas others have evolved into more general discussion lists that are less focused on problem solving.

用户可以编辑问题与回答，使其随代码和事实的变化而保持准确、有用。结果是，一些邮件列表已被 YAQS 取代，而另一些则演变为更通用的讨论列表，不再那么聚焦于解决问题。

Scaling Your Knowledge: You Always Have Something to Teach · 扩展你的知识：你总有可教之物

Teaching is not limited to experts, nor is expertise a binary state in which you are either a novice or an expert. Expertise is a multidimensional vector of what you know: everyone has varying levels of expertise across different areas. This is one of the reasons why diversity is critical to organizational success: different people bring different perspectives and expertise to the table (see Chapter 4). Google engineers teach others in a variety of ways, such as office hours, giving tech talks, teaching classes, writing documentation, and reviewing code.

教学并不限于专家，专长也不是一种“要么新手、要么专家”的二元状态。专长是一个关于你所知的多维向量：每个人在不同领域都有不同水平的专长。这正是为什么多样性对组织成功至关重要的原因之一：不同的人把不同的视角与专长带到桌面上（见第 4 章）。Google 工程师以多种方式教别人，例如办公时间答疑、做技术演讲、授课、写文档和评审代码。

Office Hours · 办公时间（Office Hours）

Sometimes it’s really important to have a human to talk to, and in those instances, office hours can be a good solution. Office hours are a regularly scheduled (typically weekly) event during which one or more people make themselves available to answer questions about a particular topic. Office hours are almost never the first choice for knowledge sharing: if you have an urgent question, it can be painful to wait for the next session for an answer; and if you’re hosting office hours, they take up time and need to be regularly promoted. That said, they do provide a way for people to talk to an expert in person. This is particularly useful if the problem is still ambiguous enough that the engineer doesn’t yet know what questions to ask (such as when they’re just starting to design a new service) or whether the problem is about something so specialized that there just isn’t documentation on it.

有时候，能有一个可以交谈的人真的很重要，在这种情况下，办公时间答疑会是一个好办法。办公时间是定期安排（通常每周一次）的活动，期间一个或多个人腾出时间，回答关于某一特定主题的问题。办公时间几乎从来不是知识共享的首选：如果你有个紧急问题，要等下一次活动才能得到答案会很煎熬；而如果你在主持办公时间，它会占用时间、还需要定期宣传。话虽如此，它确实提供了一种让人当面与专家交谈的方式。当问题还足够模糊、工程师还不知道该问什么问题时（比如刚开始设计一个新服务时），或者问题太过专门、根本没有相关文档时，这种方式尤其有用。

Google has a robust culture of both internal and external tech talks and classes. Our engEDU (Engineering Education) team focuses on providing Computer Science education to many audiences, ranging from Google engineers to students around the world. At a more grassroots level, our g2g (Googler2Googler) program lets Googlers

Tech talks typically consist of a speaker presenting directly to an audience. Classes, on the other hand, can have a lecture component but often center on in-class exercises and therefore require more active participation from attendees.     主题受益于有老师在场答疑、提供个性化帮助。如果学生无需引导帮助也能轻松自学，那文档或录像这类自助媒介效率更高。

Documentation · 文档

Documentation is written knowledge whose primary goal is to help its readers learn something. Not all written knowledge is necessarily documentation, although it can be useful as a paper trail. For example, it’s possible to find an answer to a problem in a mailing list thread, but the primary goal of the original question on the thread was to seek answers, and only secondarily to document the discussion for others.

文档是书面知识，其首要目标是帮助读者学到东西。并非所有书面知识都必然是文档，尽管作为书面记录它可能有用。例如，你可能在一个邮件列表线程里找到某个问题的答案，但那个线程中原问题的首要目标是寻求答案，把讨论记录下来供他人参考只是次要目的。

In this section, we focus on spotting opportunities for contributing to and creating formal documentation, from small things like fixing a typo to larger efforts such as documenting tribal knowledge. (For a more comprehensive discussion of documentation, see Chapter 10.)

Updating documentation · 更新文档

The first time you learn something is the best time to see ways that the existing documentation and training materials can be improved. By the time you’ve absorbed and understood a new process or system, you might have forgotten what was difficult or what simple steps were missing from the “Getting Started” documentation. At this stage, if you find a mistake or omission in the documentation, fix it! Leave the campground cleaner than you found it, and try to update the documents yourself, even when that documentation is owned by a different part of the organization. At Google, engineers feel empowered to update documentation regardless of who owns it—and we often do—even if the fix is as small as correcting a typo. This level of community upkeep increased notably with the introduction of g3doc, which made it much easier for Googlers to find a documentation owner to review their suggestion. It also leaves an auditable trail of change history no different than that for code.

你第一次学到某样东西的时候，正是发现现有文档与培训材料可以如何改进的最佳时机。等你吸收、理解了一个新流程或系统之后，你也许已经忘了当时哪里困难、“入门”文档里漏了哪些简单步骤。在这个阶段，如果你在文档里发现错误或遗漏，就修掉它！把营地收拾得比你发现时更干净，并且尽量自己更新文档——哪怕那份文档归组织的另一个部门所有。在 Google，工程师感到有权更新文档，无论它归谁——我们也经常这么做——哪怕只是改一个错别字。随着 g3doc 的引入，这种社区维护水平显著提高，它让 Googler 更容易找到文档所有者来评审自己的建议。它还留下了一条与代码无异、可审计的变更历史轨迹。

Creating documentation · 创建文档

As your proficiency grows, write your own documentation and update existing docs. For example, if you set up a new development flow, document the steps. You can then make it easier for others to follow in your path by pointing them to your document. Even better, make it easier for people to find the document themselves. Any sufficiently undiscoverable or unsearchable documentation might as well not exist. This is another area in which g3doc shines because the documentation is predictably located right next to the source code, as opposed to off in an (unfindable) document or webpage somewhere.

随着你熟练度增长，写你自己的文档、更新已有文档。例如，如果你搭建了一套新的开发流程，就把步骤记录下来。然后你可以通过把别人引向你的文档，让他们更容易走你的路。更进一步，让人们更容易自己找到这份文档。任何足够难以发现、难以搜索的文档，简直就等于不存在。这正是 g3doc 出彩的又一个地方：文档可以预期地就放在源代码旁边，而不是塞在某个找不到的文档或网页角落里。

最后，确保有反馈机制。如果读者没有简单直接的方式来指出文档过时或不准确，他们很可能懒得告诉任何人，而下一个新人就会撞上同样的问

lem. People are more willing to contribute changes if they feel that someone will actually notice and consider their suggestions. At Google, you can file a documentation bug directly from the document itself. In addition, Googlers can easily leave comments on g3doc pages. Other Googlers can see and respond to these comments and, because leaving a comment automatically files a bug for the documentation owner, the reader doesn’t need to figure out who to contact.

题。如果人们感到真的会有人注意并考虑他们的建议，他们会更愿意贡献改动。在 Google，你可以直接从文档本身提交一个文档 bug。此外，Googler 可以方便地在 g3doc 页面上留言。其他 Googler 能看到并回应这些评论；而且由于留言会自动为文档所有者建一个 bug，读者不必自己去搞清该联系谁。

Promoting documentation · 推广文档

Traditionally, encouraging engineers to document their work can be difficult. Writing documentation takes time and effort that could be spent on coding, and the benefits that result from that work are not immediate and are mostly reaped by others. Asymmetrical trade-offs like these are good for the organization as a whole given that many people can benefit from the time investment of a few, but without good incentives, it can be challenging to encourage such behavior. We discuss some of these structural incentives in the section “Incentives and recognition.”

传统上，鼓励工程师把工作写进文档可能很困难。写文档要花本可用于写代码的时间与精力，而这项工作带来的好处并不立竿见影，且大多被他人收获。像这样不对称的权衡，对整个组织是有利的——因为许多人能从少数人的时间投入中受益——但如果没有良好的激励，鼓励这种行为就很有挑战。我们在“激励与认可”一节讨论其中一些结构性激励。

However, a document author can often directly benefit from writing documentation. Suppose that team members always ask you for help debugging certain kinds of production failures. Documenting your procedures requires an upfront investment of time, but after that work is done, you can save time in the future by pointing team members to the documentation and providing hands-on help only when needed.

然而，写文档往往也能让文档作者本人直接受益。假设团队成员总是找你帮忙调试某类生产故障。把你的流程记录下来需要前期投入时间，但这项工作完成后，你今后就可以把团队成员引向文档、只在需要时才提供手把手帮助，从而节省时间。

Writing documentation also helps your team and organization scale. First, the information in the documentation becomes canonicalized as a reference: team members can refer to the shared document and even update it themselves. Second, the canonicalization may spread outside the team. Perhaps some parts of the documentation are not unique to the team’s configuration and become useful for other teams looking to resolve similar problems.

写文档还能帮助你的团队和组织扩展。首先，文档中的信息会作为参考被规范化：团队成员可以引用这份共享文档，甚至自己更新它。其次，这种规范化可能扩散到团队之外。也许文档中的某些部分并非该团队配置所独有，从而对其他想解决类似问题的团队也变得有用。

Code · 代码

At a meta level, code is knowledge, so the very act of writing code can be considered a form of knowledge transcription. Although knowledge sharing might not be a direct intent of production code, it is often an emergent side effect, which can be facilitated by code readability and clarity. Code documentation is one way to share knowledge; clear documentation not only benefits consumers of the library, but also future maintainers. Similarly, implementation comments transmit knowledge across time: you’re writing these comments expressly for the sake of future readers (including Future You!). In terms of trade-offs, code comments are subject to the same downsides as general documentation: they need to be actively maintained or they can quickly become out of date, as anyone who has ever read a comment that directly contradicts the code can attest.

在一个元层面上，代码就是知识，因此写代码这个动作本身就可以被视为一种知识转写。尽管知识共享未必是生产代码的直接意图，但它往往是一种涌现的副产品，而代码的可读性与清晰度可以促成这一点。代码文档是共享知识的一种方式；清晰的文档不仅惠及库的使用者，也惠及未来的维护者。同样，实现注释是在时间中传递知识：你写这些注释正是为了未来的读者（包括未来的你！）。在权衡方面，代码注释面临与一般文档相同的缺点：它们需要被主动维护，否则很快就会过时——任何读到过一条与代码直接矛盾的注释的人都能作证。

Code reviews (see Chapter 9) are often a learning opportunity for both author(s) and reviewer(s). For example, a reviewer’s suggestion might introduce the author to a new testing pattern, or a reviewer might learn of a new library by seeing the author use it in their code. Google standardizes mentoring through code review with the readability process, as detailed in the case study at the end of this chapter.

代码评审（见第 9 章）对作者和评审者双方来说，往往都是学习机会。例如，评审者的建议可能让作者接触到一种新的测试模式，或者评审者通过看到作者在代码中使用某个库而了解到一个新库。Google 通过 readability 流程把基于代码评审的导师制标准化，本章末尾的案例研究会详细介绍。

Scaling Your Organization’s Knowledge · 扩展组织的知识

Ensuring that expertise is appropriately shared across the organization becomes more difficult as the organization grows. Some things, like culture, are important at every stage of growth, whereas others, like establishing canonical sources of information, might be more beneficial for more mature organizations.

随着组织成长，确保专长在整个组织内被恰当分享会变得更困难。有些东西（如文化）在成长的每个阶段都重要，而另一些东西（如建立权威信息源）可能对更成熟的组织更有益。

Cultivating a Knowledge-Sharing Culture · 培育知识共享文化

Organizational culture is the squishy human thing that many companies treat as an afterthought. But at Google, we believe that focusing on the culture and environment first results in better outcomes than focusing on only the output—such as the code—of that environment. Making major organizational shifts is difficult, and countless books have been written on the topic. We don’t pretend to have all the answers, but we can share specific steps Google has taken to create a culture that promotes learning. (See the book Work Rules! for a more in-depth examination of Google’s culture.)

组织文化是那件软绵绵的“人的事”，许多公司都把它当事后补充。但在 Google，我们相信先聚焦文化与环境，比只聚焦环境的产出（比如代码）能带来更好的结果。做出重大的组织转变很难，关于这个话题的书已汗牛充栋。我们并不假装拥有全部答案，但我们可以分享 Google 为培育学习文化所采取的具体步骤。（更深入考察 Google 文化，见《Work Rules!》一书。）

原书第 84 页

Respect · 尊重

The bad behavior of just a few individuals can make an entire team or community unwelcoming. In such an environment, novices learn to take their questions elsewhere, and potential new experts stop trying and don’t have room to grow. In the worst cases, the group reduces to its most toxic members. It can be difficult to recover from this state. Knowledge sharing can and should be done with kindness and respect. In tech, tolerance—or worse, reverence—of the “brilliant jerk” is both pervasive and harmful, but being an expert and being kind are not mutually exclusive. The Leadership section of Google’s software engineering job ladder outlines this clearly:

仅仅几个人的不良行为，就能让整个团队或社区变得不受欢迎。在这种环境里，新手学会把问题带去别处，潜在的新专家也停止尝试、没有成长空间。在最坏的情况下，群体会退化成由其中最毒的成员定义。要从这种状态恢复过来可能很难。知识共享能够、也应当带着善意与尊重来进行。在科技界，对“聪明的混蛋”的容忍——甚至更糟，崇拜——既普遍又有害，但做专家与做个好人并不互斥。Google 软件工程师职级 ladder 的“领导力”部分把这一点说得很清楚：

Although a measure of technical leadership is expected at higher levels, not
all leadership is directed at technical problems. Leaders improve the quality
of the people around them, improve the team’s psychological safety, create a
culture of teamwork and collaboration, defuse tensions within the team, set an
example of Google’s culture and values, and make Google a more vibrant and
exciting place to work. Jerks are not good leaders.

This expectation is modeled by senior leadership: Urs Hölzle (Senior Vice President of Technical Infrastructure) and Ben Treynor Sloss (Vice President, Founder of Google SRE) wrote a regularly cited internal document (“No Jerks”) about why Googlers should care about respectful behavior at work and what to do about it.

这一期望由高层领导以身作则：Urs Hölzle（技术基础设施高级副总裁）与 Ben Treynor Sloss（副总裁、Google SRE 创始人）写过一篇常被引用的内部文档（“不许有混蛋”），阐述为什么 Googler 应当在乎工作中的尊重行为、以及该怎么做。

Incentives and recognition · 激励与认可

Good culture must be actively nurtured, and encouraging a culture of knowledge sharing requires a commitment to recognizing and rewarding it at a systemic level. It’s a common mistake for organizations to pay lip service to a set of values while actively rewarding behavior that does not enforce those values. People react to incentives over platitudes, and so it’s important to put your money where your mouth is by putting in place a system of compensation and awards. Google uses a variety of recognition mechanisms, from company-wide standards such as performance review and promotion criteria to peer-to-peer awards between Googlers.

好的文化必须主动培育，而鼓励知识共享文化，需要在系统层面对其给予认可与奖励的承诺。一个常见错误是：组织口头上标榜一套价值观，实际却在奖励那些并不践行这些价值观的行为。人们对激励的反应胜过对空话的反应，因此重要的是言行一致，建立一套薪酬与奖励制度。Google 使用多种认可机制，从绩效评估、晋升标准这样的全公司标准，到 Googler 之间的同侪奖励，不一而足。

Our software engineering ladder, which we use to calibrate rewards like compensation and promotion across the company, encourages engineers to share knowledge by noting these expectations explicitly. At more senior levels, the ladder explicitly calls out the importance of wider influence, and this expectation increases as seniority increases. At the highest levels, examples of leadership include the following:

我们的软件工程职级 ladder 用于在全公司校准薪酬、晋升等奖励，它通过明确写出这些期望来鼓励工程师共享知识。在更高级别，ladder 明确点出更广泛影响力的重要性，而且这一期望随资历升高而增强。在最高级别，领导力的例子包括：

  • Growing future leaders by serving as mentors to junior staff, helping them develop both technically and in their Google role.

    通过担任初级员工的导师来培养未来的领导者，帮助他们在技术上和在 Google 的角色上都获得发展。

原书第 85 页

  • Sustaining and developing the software community at Google via code and design reviews, engineering education and development, and expert guidance to others in the field.

    通过代码与设计评审、工程教育培训，以及向该领域其他人提供专家指导，维系并发展 Google 的软件社区。

(See Chapters 5 and 6 for more on leadership.)

（关于领导力的更多内容，见第 5、6 章。）

Job ladder expectations are a top-down way to direct a culture, but culture is also formed from the bottom up. At Google, the peer bonus program is one way we embrace the bottom-up culture. Peer bonuses are a monetary award and formal recognition that any Googler can bestow on any other Googler for above-and-beyond work. For example, when Ravi sends a peer bonus to Julia for being a top contributor to a mailing list—regularly answering questions that benefit many readers—he is publicly recognizing her knowledge-sharing work and its impact beyond her team. Because peer bonuses are employee driven, not management driven, they can have an important and powerful grassroots effect. Similar to peer bonuses are kudos: public acknowledgement of contributions (typically smaller in impact or effort than those meriting a peer bonus) that boost the visibility of peer-to-peer contributions. When a Googler gives another Googler a peer bonus or kudos, they can choose to copy additional groups or individuals on the award email, boosting recognition of the peer’s work. It’s also common for the recipient’s manager to forward the award email to the team to celebrate one another’s achievements. A system in which people can formally and easily recognize their peers is a powerful tool for encouraging peers to keep doing the awesome things they do. It’s not the bonus that matters: it’s the peer acknowledgement.

职级 ladder 期望是自上而下引导文化的一种方式，但文化也是自下而上形成的。在 Google，同侪奖金计划是我们拥抱自下而上文化的一种方式。同侪奖金是一笔金钱奖励与正式认可，任何 Googler 都可以因某项超出本分的工作授予另一位 Googler。例如，当 Ravi 因为 Julia 是某个邮件列表的顶级贡献者——经常回答让许多读者受益的问题——而送她一笔同侪奖金时，他就是在公开认可她的知识共享工作及其超越她团队的影响。由于同侪奖金是员工驱动、而非管理层驱动的，它能产生重要而强大的草根效应。与同侪奖金类似的是 kudos（公开点赞）：对贡献的公开认可（影响或投入通常比值得同侪奖金的要小一些），用以提升同侪间贡献的可见度。当一位 Googler 给另一位同侪奖金或 kudos 时，他可以选择在奖励邮件上抄送更多群组或个人，从而提升对该同侪工作的认可。获奖者的经理把奖励邮件转发给团队、共同庆祝彼此的成就，也很常见。一个让人们能正式、方便地认可同侪的系统，是鼓励同侪继续做那些了不起之事的有力工具。重要的不是那笔奖金，而是同侪的认可。

Establishing Canonical Sources of Information · 建立权威信息源

Canonical sources of information are centralized, company-wide corpuses of information that provide a way to standardize and propagate expert knowledge. They work best for information that is relevant to all engineers within the organization, which is otherwise prone to information islands. For example, a guide to setting up a

权威信息源是集中式、全公司范围的信息库，提供了一种标准化并传播专家知识的方式。它们最适用于与组织内所有工程师都相关、否则容易陷入信息孤岛的信息。例如，一份搭建基础开发工作流的指南应当被权威化；而一份运行本地 Frobber 实例的指南，则只与在 Frobber 上工作的工程师相关。建立权威信息源比维护团队文档这类更局部的信息需要更高投入，但也有更广泛的收益。为整个组织提供集中式参考，让广泛需要的信息更容易、更可预期地被找到，并counter 多个团队在解决类似问题时各自产出（往往相互冲突）的指南所带来的信息碎片化问题。

原书第 86 页

basic developer workflow should be made canonical, whereas a guide for running a local Frobber instance is more relevant just to the engineers working on Frobber. Establishing canonical sources of information requires higher investment than maintaining more localized information such as team documentation, but it also has broader benefits. Providing centralized references for the entire organization makes broadly required information easier and more predictable to find and counters problems with information fragmentation that can arise when multiple teams grappling with similar problems produce their own—often conflicting—guides. Because canonical information is highly visible and intended to provide a shared understanding at the organizational level, it’s important that the content is actively maintained and vetted by subject matter experts. The more complex a topic, the more critical it is that canonical content has explicit owners. Well-meaning readers might see that something is out of date but lack the expertise to make the significant structural changes needed to fix it, even if tooling makes it easy to suggest updates. Creating and maintaining centralized, canonical sources of information is expensive and time consuming, and not all content needs to be shared at an organizational level. When considering how much effort to invest in this resource, consider your audience. Who benefits from this information? You? Your team? Your product area? All engineers?

由于权威信息可见度高、意在组织层面提供共同理解，内容必须被主动维护、并经主题专家审核。主题越复杂，权威内容有明确所有者就越关键。善意的读者也许能看出某样东西过时了，却缺乏做出修复所需重大结构性改动的专长——即便工具让“建议更新”变得容易。创建并维护集中式权威信息源代价高昂、耗时，而且并非所有内容都需要在组织层面共享。在考虑为这项资源投入多少时，想想你的受众：谁会从这些信息中受益？你自己？你的团队？你的产品领域？还是所有工程师？

Developer guides · 开发者指南

Google has a broad and deep set of official guidance for engineers, including style guides, official software engineering best practices, guides for code review and testing, and Tips of the Week (TotW). The corpus of information is so large that it’s impractical to expect engineers to read it all end to end, much less be able to absorb so much information at once. Instead, a human expert already familiar with a guideline can send a link to a fellow engineer, who then can read the reference and learn more. The expert saves time by not needing to personally explain a company-wide practice, and the learner now knows that there is a canonical source of trustworthy information that they can access whenever necessary. Such a process scales knowledge because it enables human experts to recognize and solve a specific information need by leveraging common, scalable resources.

Google 为工程师提供了一整套广博而深入的官方指南，包括风格指南、官方软件工程最佳实践、代码评审与测试指南，以及每周一tip（TotW）。信息库如此庞大，指望工程师从头到尾读完并不现实，更别说一次吸收这么多信息。相反，一位已经熟悉某条指南的人类专家可以把链接发给另一位工程师，后者再去阅读参考、了解更多。专家免去了亲自解释一项全公司实践的麻烦，节省了时间；学习者则知道了存在一个权威、可信的信息源，可在需要时随时查阅。这样一个过程让知识得以扩展，因为它使人类专家能够借助通用、可扩展的资源，来识别并解决某个具体的信息需求。

go/ links · go/ 链接

go/ links (sometimes referred to as goto/ links) are Google’s internal URL shortener. Most Google-internal references have at least one internal go/ link. For example, “go/spanner” provides information about Spanner, “go/python” is Google’s Python developer guide. The content can live in any repository (g3doc, Google Drive, Google Sites, etc.), but having a go/ link that points to it provides a predictable, memorable way to access it. This yields some nice benefits:

go/ 链接（有时也称 goto/ 链接）是 Google 内部的 URL 缩短服务。大多数 Google 内部引用都至少有一个内部 go/ 链接。例如，“go/spanner”提供关于 Spanner 的信息，“go/python”是 Google 的 Python 开发者指南。内容可以放在任何仓库里（g3doc、Google Drive、Google Sites 等），但有一个指向它的 go/ 链接，就提供了一种可预期、好记的访问方式。这带来了一些不错的好处：

  • go/ links are so short that it’s easy to share them in conversation (“You should check out go/frobber!”). This is much easier than having to go find a link and then send a message to all interested parties. Having a low-friction way to share references makes it more likely that that knowledge will be shared in the first place.

    go/ 链接极短，在对话中分享很容易（“你该看看 go/frobber！”）。这比去找到链接、再给所有相关人发消息容易得多。有了一种低摩擦的引用分享方式，知识从一开始就更可能被分享出去。

  • go/ links provide a permalink to the content, even if the underlying URL changes. When an owner moves content to a different repository, they can simply update the go/ link’s target URL. The go/ link itself remains unchanged.

    go/ 链接为内容提供了永久链接，即便底层 URL 变了。当所有者把内容搬到另一个仓库时，只需更新 go/ 链接的目标 URL 即可，go/ 链接本身保持不变。

go/ links are so ingrained into Google culture that a virtuous cycle has emerged: a Googler looking for information about Frobber will likely first check go/frobber. If the go/ link doesn’t point to the Frobber Developer Guide (as expected), the Googler will generally configure the link themselves. As a result, Googlers can usually guess the correct go/ link on the first try.

go/ 链接已深深嵌入 Google 文化，以至于形成了一个良性循环：一个想了解 Frobber 的 Googler，很可能先查 go/frobber。如果这个 go/ 链接没有（像预期那样）指向 Frobber 开发者指南，这位 Googler 通常会自己去配置这个链接。结果是，Googler 往往第一次就能猜对正确的 go/ 链接。

Codelabs · Codelab 实操教程

Google codelabs are guided, hands-on tutorials that teach engineers new concepts or processes by combining explanations, working best-practice example code, and code exercises. A canonical collection of codelabs for technologies broadly used across Google is available at go/codelab. These codelabs go through several rounds of formal review and testing before publication. Codelabs are an interesting halfway point between static documentation and instructor-led classes, and they share the best and worst features of each. Their hands-on nature makes them more engaging than traditional documentation, but engineers can still access them on demand and complete them on their own; but they are expensive to maintain and are not tailored to the learner’s specific needs.

Google codelab 是引导式、动手实操的教程，通过结合讲解、可运行的最佳实践示例代码和代码练习，来教工程师新概念或新流程。Google 内部广泛使用技术的权威 codelab 合集可在 go/codelab 找到。这些 codelab 在发布前要经过几轮正式评审与测试。Codelab 是介于静态文档与讲师授课之间一个有趣的中间形态，兼有两者最好与最差的特点。其实操本质让它比传统文档更有吸引力，工程师仍可按需访问、独立完成；但它维护成本高昂，也并不针对学习者的具体需求定制。

原书第 88 页

Static analysis · 静态分析

Static analysis tools are a powerful way to share best practices that can be checked programmatically. Every programming language has its own particular static analysis tools, but they have the same general purpose: to alert code authors and reviewers to ways in which code can be improved to follow style and best practices. Some tools go one step further and offer to automatically apply those improvements to the code. (See Chapter 20 for details on static analysis tools and how they’re used at Google.)

静态分析工具是分享“可被程序化检查的最佳实践”的有力方式。每种编程语言都有自己特定的静态分析工具，但它们的总体目的相同：提醒代码作者和评审者代码可以在哪些方面改进、以遵循风格与最佳实践。有些工具更进一步，还会自动把这些改进应用到代码上。（静态分析工具及其在 Google 的使用细节，见第 20 章。）

Setting up static analysis tools requires an upfront investment, but as soon as they are in place, they scale efficiently. When a check for a best practice is added to a tool, every engineer using that tool becomes aware of that best practice. This also frees up engineers to teach other things: the time and effort that would have gone into manually teaching the (now automated) best practice can instead be used to teach something else. Static analysis tools augment engineers’ knowledge. They enable an organization to apply more best practices and apply them more consistently than would otherwise be possible.

搭建静态分析工具需要前期投入，但一旦就位，就能高效扩展。当一条最佳实践的检查被加进工具时，使用该工具的每一位工程师都会知道这条最佳实践。这也把工程师解放出来去教别的东西：原本要手动教那条（如今已自动化的）最佳实践的时间与精力，可以转而用来教别的。静态分析工具增强了工程师的知识，让一个组织能够应用更多最佳实践、而且应用得比其他方式更一致。

Staying in the Loop · 保持在信息圈中

Some information is critical to do one’s job, such as knowing how to do a typical development workflow. Other information, such as updates on popular productivity tools, is less critical but still useful. For this type of knowledge, the formality of the information sharing medium depends on the importance of the information being delivered. For example, users expect official documentation to be kept up to date, but typically have no such expectation for newsletter content, which therefore requires less maintenance and upkeep from the owner.

有些信息对完成工作至关重要，比如知道如何进行典型的开发工作流。另一些信息（比如热门生产力工具的更新）则没那么关键、但仍有用。对这类知识，信息共享媒介的正式程度取决于所传递信息的重要性。例如，用户期望官方文档保持最新，但对通讯简报的内容通常没有这种期望，因此后者对所有者来说需要的维护与打理也更少。

Newsletters · 通讯简报

Google has a number of company-wide newsletters that are sent to all engineers, including EngNews (engineering news), Ownd (Privacy/Security news), and Google’s Greatest Hits (report of the most interesting outages of the quarter). These are a good way to communicate information that is of interest to engineers but isn’t mission critical. For this type of update, we’ve found that newsletters get better engagement when they are sent less frequently and contain more useful, interesting content. Otherwise, newsletters can be perceived as spam. Even though most Google newsletters are sent via email, some are more creative in their distribution. Testing on the Toilet (testing tips) and Learning on the Loo (produ-

Google 有若干发给全体工程师的全公司通讯简报，包括 EngNews（工程新闻）、Ownd（隐私/安全新闻）以及 Google’s Greatest Hits（本季度最有意思的宕机报告）。这些是传达工程师感兴趣、但并非任务关键信息的好方式。对这类更新，我们发现通讯简报发送频率更低、内容更有用有趣时，参与度更高；否则就会被当作垃圾邮件。尽管 Google 大多数通讯通过邮件发送，有些在分发上更有创意：《Testing on the Toilet》（测试小贴士）和《Learning on the Loo》（生产力小贴士）是单页简报，贴在厕所隔间里。这种独特的分发媒介让它们从其他简报中脱颖而出，而且所有期次都在线存档。

ctivity tips) are single-page newsletters posted inside toilet stalls. This unique delivery medium helps the Testing on the Toilet and Learning on the Loo stand out from other newsletters, and all issues are archived online. (See Chapter 11 for a history of how Testing on the Toilet came to be.)

（《Testing on the Toilet》的由来历史，见第 11 章。）

Communities · 社区

Googlers like to form cross-organizational communities around various topics to share knowledge. These open channels make it easier to learn from others outside your immediate circle and avoid information islands and duplication. Google Groups are especially popular: Google has thousands of internal groups with varying levels of formality. Some are dedicated to troubleshooting; others, like the Code Health group, are more for discussion and guidance. Internal Google+ is also popular among Googlers as a source of informal information because people will post interesting technical breakdowns or details about projects they are working on.

Googler 喜欢围绕各种主题组建跨组织的社区来共享知识。这些开放的渠道让你更容易向自己小圈子之外的人学习，避免信息孤岛与重复。Google Groups 尤其流行：Google 有数千个内部群组，正式程度不一。有些专注于排障；另一些（如 Code Health 群组）更偏向讨论与指导。内部 Google+ 在 Googler 中也很受欢迎，作为非正式信息来源，因为人们会发布有趣的技术拆解或他们正在做的项目细节。

Readability: Standardized Mentorship Through Code Review · Readability：通过代码评审实现标准化导师制

At Google, “readability” refers to more than just code readability; it is a standardized, Google-wide mentorship process for disseminating programming language best practices. Readability covers a wide breadth of expertise, including but not limited to language idioms, code structure, API design, appropriate use of common libraries, documentation, and test coverage. Readability started as a one-person effort. In Google’s early days, Craig Silverstein (employee ID #3) would sit down in person with every new hire and do a line-by-line “readability review” of their first major code commit. It was a nitpicky review that covered everything from ways the code could be improved to whitespace conventions. This gave Google’s codebase a uniform appearance but, more important, it taught best practices, highlighted what shared infrastructure was available, and showed new hires what it’s like to write code at Google. Inevitably, Google’s hiring rate grew beyond what one person could keep up with. So many engineers found the process valuable that they volunteered their own time to scale the program. Today, around 20% of Google engineers are participating in the readability process at any given time, as either reviewers or code authors.

在 Google，“readability”不仅指代码可读性；它是一个标准化、全 Google 范围的导师制流程，用于传播编程语言最佳实践。Readability 覆盖广泛的专长领域，包括但不限于语言惯用法、代码结构、API 设计、常用库的恰当使用、文档与测试覆盖率。Readability 始于一个人的努力。在 Google 早期，Craig Silverstein（员工编号 #3）会亲自和每位新员工坐下来，对他们第一次重要代码提交逐行做一次“readability 评审”。那是一次吹毛求疵的评审，涵盖从代码可改进之处到空白字符约定的一切。这让 Google 的代码库外观统一，但更重要的是，它教会了最佳实践、点明了有哪些共享基础设施可用，并向新员工展示了在 Google 写代码是什么样子。不可避免地，Google 的招聘速度增长到一个人忙不过来的程度。有如此多工程师发现这个流程有价值，以至于他们自愿抽出时间来扩展这个计划。如今，任何时刻都有约 20% 的 Google 工程师以评审者或代码作者的身份参与 readability 流程。

What Is the Readability Process? · Readability 流程是什么？

Code review is mandatory at Google. Every changelist (CL) requires readability approval, which indicates that someone who has readability certification for that language has approved the CL. Certified authors implicitly provide readability approval of their own CLs; otherwise, one or more qualified reviewers must explicitly give readability approval for the CL. This requirement was added after Google grew to a point where it was no longer possible to enforce that every engineer received code reviews that taught best practices to the desired rigor. (See Chapter 9 for an overview of the Google code review process and what Approval means in this context.)

在 Google，代码评审是强制的。每个变更列表（CL）都需要 readability 批准，即某位持有该语言 readability 认证的人批准了该 CL。有认证的作者隐式地为自己的 CL 提供 readability 批准；否则，就必须有一位或多位合格评审者显式地为 CL 给出 readability 批准。这一要求是在 Google 长大到无法再强制“每位工程师都接受到具有应有严谨度、能传授最佳实践的代码评审”之后才加上的。（Google 代码评审流程概览及此处“批准”的含义，见第 9 章。）

Within Google, having readability certification is commonly referred to as “having readability” for a language. Engineers with readability have demonstrated that they consistently write clear, idiomatic, and maintainable code that exemplifies Google’s best practices and coding style for a given language. They do this by submitting CLs through the readability process, during which a centralized group of readability reviewers review the CLs and give feedback on how much it demonstrates the various areas of mastery. As authors internalize the readability guidelines, they receive fewer and fewer comments on their CLs until they eventually graduate from the process and formally receive readability. Readability brings increased responsibility: engineers with readability are trusted to continue to apply their knowledge to their own code and to act as reviewers for other engineers’ code.

在 Google 内部，持有 readability 认证通常被称为“拥有某语言的 readability”。拥有 readability 的工程师已经证明：他们能持续写出清晰、地道、可维护的代码，成为 Google 该语言最佳实践与编码风格的典范。他们是通过把 CL 提交进 readability 流程来做到这一点的——在此过程中，一个集中的 readability 评审者小组评审这些 CL，并就其在各精通领域上的体现程度给出反馈。随着作者把 readability 指南内化，他们的 CL 收到的评论越来越少，直到最终从流程毕业、正式获得 readability。Readability 也带来更大的责任：拥有 readability 的工程师被信任把自己的知识持续应用于自身代码，并担任其他工程师代码的评审者。

Around 1 to 2% of Google engineers are readability reviewers. All reviewers are volunteers, and anyone with readability is welcome to self-nominate to become a readability reviewer. Readability reviewers are held to the highest standards because they are expected not just to have deep language expertise, but also an aptitude for teaching through code review. They are expected to treat readability as first and foremost a mentoring and cooperative process, not a gatekeeping or adversarial one. Readability reviewers and CL authors alike are encouraged to have discussions during the review process. Reviewers provide relevant citations for their comments so that authors can learn about the rationales that went into the style guidelines (“Chesterton’s fence”). If the rationale for any given guideline is unclear, authors should ask for clarification (“ask questions”).

Google 工程师中约有 1% 到 2% 是 readability 评审者。所有评审者都是志愿者，任何拥有 readability 的人都欢迎自荐成为 readability 评审者。Readability 评审者被以最高标准要求，因为他们不仅要有深厚的语言专长，还要有通过代码评审进行教学的天赋。他们应当把 readability 首先当作一个导师式、合作式的流程，而不是把关或对抗式的流程。readability 评审者与 CL 作者都被鼓励在评审过程中展开讨论。评审者为自己的评论提供相关引用，好让作者了解风格指南背后的道理（“切斯特顿的栅栏”）。如果某条指南背后的道理不清楚，作者应当要求澄清（“多提问”）。

原书第 91 页

Readability is deliberately a human-driven process that aims to scale knowledge in a standardized yet personalized way. As a complementary blend of written and tribal knowledge, readability combines the advantages of written documentation, which can be accessed with citable references, with the advantages of expert human reviewers, who know which guidelines to cite. Canonical guidelines and language recommendations are comprehensively documented—which is good!—but the corpus of information is so large that it can be overwhelming, especially to newcomers.

Readability 刻意是一个由人驱动的流程，旨在以一种标准化却又个性化的方式扩展知识。作为书面知识与部落知识的互补融合，readability 把“可被引用查阅的书面文档”的优势，与“知道该引用哪条指南的人类专家评审者”的优势结合起来。权威指南与语言建议被全面记录下来——这很好！——但信息库如此庞大，以至于可能让人望而生畏，尤其是对新人。

Why Have This Process? · 为什么要有这个流程？

Code is read far more than it is written, and this effect is magnified at Google’s scale and in our (very large) monorepo. Any engineer can look at and learn from the wealth of knowledge that is the code of other teams, and powerful tools like Kythe make it easy to find references throughout the entire codebase (see Chapter 17). An important feature of documented best practices (see Chapter 8) is that they provide consistent standards for all Google code to follow. Readability is both an enforcement and propagation mechanism for these standards.

代码被阅读的次数远多于被编写的次数，而这种效应在 Google 的规模和我们（非常大的）单一代码仓里被放大。任何工程师都能查看其他团队代码这座知识宝库并从中学习，而像 Kythe 这样强大的工具让在整个代码库中查找引用变得容易（见第 17 章）。成文最佳实践（见第 8 章）的一个重要特点是：它们为所有 Google 代码提供了一套一致遵循的标准。Readability 既是这些标准的执行机制，也是传播机制。

One of the primary advantages of the readability program is that it exposes engineers to more than just their own team’s tribal knowledge. To earn readability in a given language, engineers must send CLs through a centralized set of readability reviewers who review code across the entire company. Centralizing the process makes a significant trade-off: the program is limited to scaling linearly rather than sublinearly with organization growth, but it makes it easier to enforce consistency, avoid islands, and avoid (often unintentional) drifting from established norms. The value of codebase-wide consistency cannot be overstated: even with tens of thousands of engineers writing code over decades, it ensures that code in a given language will look similar across the corpus. This enables readers to focus on what the code does rather than being distracted by why it looks different than code that they’re used to. Large-scale change authors (see Chapter 22) can more easily make changes across the entire monorepo, crossing the boundaries of thousands of teams. People can change teams and be confident that the way that the new team uses a given language is not drastically different than their previous team.

readability 计划的主要优势之一，是让工程师接触到超越自己团队部落知识的东西。要获得某语言的 readability，工程师必须把 CL 送交一组集中的 readability 评审者，他们评审全公司范围的代码。把流程集中化是一个重大权衡：这个计划只能随组织增长线性扩展、而不能亚线性扩展，但它让执行一致性、避免孤岛、避免（往往是无心地）偏离既定规范变得更容易。全代码库一致性的价值怎么强调都不为过：即便有数万工程师在数十年间写代码，它也能确保某语言的代码在整个语料库中看起来相似。这让读者能专注于代码做什么，而不是被“它为什么和我习惯的代码长得不一样”所分心。大规模变更的作者（见第 22 章）能更容易地跨整个单一代码仓、跨越数千个团队的边界做变更。人们换团队时可以确信：新团队使用某语言的方式，与他们之前的团队不会有天壤之别。

原书第 92 页

These benefits come with some costs: readability is a heavyweight process compared to other mediums like documentation and classes because it is mandatory and enforced by Google tooling (see Chapter 19). These costs are nontrivial and include the following:

这些好处也伴随着一些成本：与文档、课程等其他媒介相比，readability 是一个重量级流程，因为它是强制的、并由 Google 工具强制执行（见第 19 章）。这些成本不可小觑，包括：

  • Increased friction for teams that do not have any team members with readability, because they need to find reviewers from outside their team to give readability approval on CLs.

    对团队中没有任何成员拥有 readability 的团队，摩擦增加，因为他们需要从团队外找评审者来为 CL 给出 readability 批准。

  • Potential for additional rounds of code review for authors who need readability review.

    对需要 readability 评审的作者，可能需要多轮代码评审。

  • Scaling disadvantages of being a human-driven process. Limited to scaling linearly to organization growth because it depends on human reviewers doing specialized code reviews.

    作为由人驱动的流程所固有的扩展性劣势：因为依赖人类评审者做专门的代码评审，它只能随组织增长线性扩展。

The question, then, is whether the benefits outweigh the costs. There’s also the factor of time: the full effect of the benefits versus the costs are not on the same timescale. The program makes a deliberate trade-off of increased short-term code-review latency and upfront costs for the long-term payoffs of higher-quality code, repository-wide code consistency, and increased engineer expertise. The longer timescale of the benefits comes with the expectation that code is written with a potential lifetime of years, if not decades.

那么问题就是：收益是否大于成本。还有时间这个因素：收益与成本的全部效应并不在同一时间尺度上。这个计划刻意做了一个权衡：用增加短期代码评审延迟与前期成本，换取更高质量代码、全仓库代码一致性、工程师专长提升这些长期回报。收益之所以放在更长的时间尺度上，是因为我们写的代码预期可能存活数年、甚至数十年。

As with most—or perhaps all—engineering processes, there’s always room for improvement. Some of the costs can be mitigated with tooling. A number of readability comments address issues that could be detected statically and commented on automatically by static analysis tooling. As we continue to invest in static analysis, readability reviewers can increasingly focus on higher-order areas, like whether a particular block of code is understandable by outside readers who are not intimately familiar with the codebase instead of automatable detections like whether a line has trailing whitespace. But aspirations aren’t enough. Readability is a controversial program: some engineers complain that it’s an unnecessary bureaucratic hurdle and a poor use of engineer time. Are readability’s trade-offs worthwhile? For the answer, we turned to our trusty Engineering Productivity Research (EPR) team.

和大多数——也许是全部——工程流程一样，它总有改进空间。其中一些成本可以用工具来缓解。许多 readability 评论所针对的问题，本可以被静态分析工具静态检测出来并自动评论。随着我们持续投资静态分析，readability 评审者可以越来越聚焦于更高阶的领域，比如某段代码是否能被不熟悉代码库的外部读者理解，而不是像“一行末尾是否有尾随空白”这种可自动化检测的问题。但光有抱负还不够。Readability 是一个有争议的计划：有些工程师抱怨它是不必要的官僚障碍、是对工程师时间的浪费。readability 的权衡值得吗？为寻求答案，我们求助于我们可靠的工程生产力研究（EPR）团队。

原书第 93 页

The EPR team performed in-depth studies of readability, including but not limited to whether people were hindered by the process, learned anything, or changed their behavior after graduating. These studies showed that readability has a net positive impact on engineering velocity. CLs by authors with readability take statistically significantly less time to review and submit than CLs by authors who do not have readability. Self-reported engineer satisfaction with their code quality—lacking more objective measures for code quality—is higher among engineers who have readability versus those who do not. A significant majority of engineers who complete the program report satisfaction with the process and find it worthwhile. They report learning from reviewers and changing their own behavior to avoid readability issues when writing and reviewing code. (For an in-depth look at this study and Google’s internal engineering productivity research, see Chapter 7.)

EPR 团队对 readability 做了深入研究，包括但不限于：人们是否被这个流程拖累、是否学到了东西、毕业后是否改变了行为。这些研究表明，readability 对工程速度有净正面影响。拥有 readability 的作者所写的 CL，其评审与提交时间在统计上显著短于没有 readability 的作者。在缺乏更客观代码质量度量的情况下，工程师自报的代码质量满意度，在拥有 readability 的工程师中高于没有的。完成该计划的工程师中，绝大多数都报告对流程满意、认为值得。他们报告从评审者那里学到了东西，并改变了自己的行为，在写代码和评审代码时避免 readability 问题。（对这项研究及 Google 内部工程生产力研究的深入考察，见第 7 章。）

Google has a very strong culture of code review, and readability is a natural extension of that culture. Readability grew from the passion of a single engineer to a formal program of human experts mentoring all Google engineers. It evolved and changed with Google’s growth, and it will continue to evolve as Google’s needs change.

Google 有着非常强的代码评审文化，readability 是这种文化的自然延伸。Readability 从一位工程师的热情，成长为一个由人类导师指导全体 Google 工程师的正式计划。它随 Google 的成长而演进、变化，也将随 Google 需求的变化而继续演进。

Conclusion · 结语

Knowledge is in some ways the most important (though intangible) capital of a software engineering organization, and sharing of that knowledge is crucial for making an organization resilient and redundant in the face of change. A culture that promotes open and honest knowledge sharing distributes that knowledge efficiently across the organization and allows that organization to scale over time. In most cases, investments into easier knowledge sharing reap manyfold dividends over the life of a company.

在某种意义上，知识是一个软件工程组织最重要（尽管无形）的资本，而共享这些知识，对于让组织在变化面前具备韧性与冗余至关重要。一种倡导开放、诚实知识共享的文化，能把知识高效地分发到整个组织，并让组织随时间扩展。在大多数情况下，投资于让知识共享更容易，会在公司的生命周期里收获成倍的回报。

TL;DRs · 要点小结（TL;DR）

  • Psychological safety is the foundation for fostering a knowledge-sharing environment.

    心理安全是培育知识共享环境的基石。

  • Start small: ask questions and write things down.

    从小处着手：提问，把东西写下来。

  • Make it easy for people to get the help they need from both human experts and documented references.

    让人们能容易地从人类专家和成文参考中获得所需帮助。

  • At a systemic level, encourage and reward those who take time to teach and broaden their expertise beyond just themselves, their team, or their organization.

    在系统层面，鼓励并奖励那些花时间教学、把专长拓展到自身、本团队或本组织之外的人。

  • There is no silver bullet: empowering a knowledge-sharing culture requires a combination of multiple strategies, and the exact mix that works best for your organization will likely change over time.

    没有银弹：赋能一种知识共享文化需要多种策略的组合，而对你组织最有效的具体配比很可能随时间变化。
